content: Nausea, derived from the Latin and Greek terms for sea-sickness, is defined as an unpleasant, painless sensation that one is about to vomit. It often serves as a symptom of an underlying condition elsewhere in the body. For example, motion sickness arises from a mismatch between perceived and actual movement, involving the inner ear's equilibrium system and visual input. When these systems provide conflicting information about the body's motion, nausea can occur, even though the stomach itself is not directly involved. Nausea is also a common side effect of many medications and can result from excessive consumption of sugary foods. In medical contexts, nausea is frequently encountered during certain chemotherapy regimens and after general anesthesia. It is also a well-known symptom of pregnancy, where mild nausea is often considered normal and not immediately alarming. Vomiting, also known as emesis, is the forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth, and sometimes the nose, caused by contractions of the gastrointestinal and thoracoabdominal wall muscles. Vomiting can have numerous causes, ranging from gastritis and poisoning to brain tumors or elevated intracranial pressure. The sensation of nausea typically precedes vomiting but does not always lead to it. Antiemetic medications are sometimes required to suppress nausea and vomiting. In severe cases where dehydration occurs, intravenous fluids may be necessary to restore fluid balance. The medical field dedicated to studying vomiting, emetics, and antiemetics is known as emetology. Historically, the term nausea originates from the classical Greek words ναυτία and ναυσία, which referred to the symptoms of sea-sickness. Descriptions of sea-sickness in medical literature from the late 19th and early 20th centuries provide insight into the evolution of the term, which has been used to describe both a specific disorder (sea-sickness) and a symptom cluster associated with other conditions. Similar patterns of terminology are observed with terms for vertigo, such as vertigine and skotodinos. Nausea and vomiting can be classified as acute or chronic. Acute vomiting, lasting from a few hours to a few days, is the most common presentation in emergency settings and requires thorough evaluation to rule out life-threatening conditions such as bowel obstruction, mesenteric ischemia, acute pancreatitis, or myocardial infarction. Chronic vomiting, persisting for weeks to months, is typically assessed in outpatient settings. The pathophysiology of nausea and vomiting is complex, involving psychological states, the central and autonomic nervous systems, gastric dysrhythmias, and the endocrine system. Each individual has a variable threshold for nausea, influenced by factors such as anxiety, anticipation, expectation, and adaptation. Stimuli triggering nausea and vomiting originate from visceral, vestibular, and chemoreceptor inputs, mediated by neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine, histamine, and acetylcholine. Life-threatening causes of nausea and vomiting include acute coronary syndrome, anaphylaxis, and heart failure. Other common causes include food allergies, food poisoning, gastroenteritis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Diagnostic evaluation of nausea and vomiting involves a detailed history, physical examination, and appropriate investigations. For example, an electrocardiogram (ECG) may be performed to rule out inferior myocardial infarction or arrhythmias. Imaging studies such as X-rays, echocardiography, and ultrasound may also be utilized to identify underlying causes.
